This would mean that some municipalities would in the future, because of continuing and unique growth of outlying areas, develop a need for specific consideration/definition or some other form of exception to a standard population-mileage formula.
Studies sometimes reveal correlates of municipal size. One such study in 1967 concluded that a given number of consumers will be served by a given mix and number of retail establishments. The market reaches are indicative of the geographical scope of physical distribution of goods within market areas and illustrate one aspect of the economic interaction and interdependency within the areas.
The movement of goods and people generated by industrial/commercial locations is totally out of proportion with the percent of land allocated for or utilized by such locations. A 1963 report on the Pittsburgh region showed that manufacturing production facilities occupied approximately 1/3 of 1% of the land in the region, or less than 15 of the region's 4,487 square miles. On an average work day, more than 1/3 of the region's work force poured into the area and the activities of the industries employing them generated more than 40% of the earned income of the region. 15/
